Very interesting find here. Unfortunately, I can't get to the New York Times article as I refuse to subscribe. I am not exactly sure what point "corporate liberal" Paul Krugman is trying to achieve, but reading some of the links around this whole story, I'll make some observations.

Monetary policy was for many years an alternative to Keynesian fiscal policy.

Monetary policy is basically the Federal Reserve controlling the money supply through buying and selling bonds, changing the reserve requirement, and adjusting the federal funds rate.

Fiscal policy is simply government spending and taxation to effect economy--surpluses in good times, deficits in bad times.

Conservatives said monetary policy was the major influence and fiscal policy didn't work, while liberals supported fiscal policy strongly and said monetary policy was largely ineffective.

Based on these articles, the partisans appear to have partially shifted positions. It certainly appears that Paul Krugman is playing a trick with his truncated graph. Rather than hiding the separation of correlation between the funds rate and the housing starts, Krugman would have done better to explain why they were so closely correlated, and what other factor has broken the correlation. I propose it is a privately-run system akin to steroidal monetary policy caused by deregulation. Banks and funds continue to create huge cash equivalents and shuffle them around from bubble to bubble manipulating the economy and affecting housing starts. Also, the increasing wealth inequality has made housing less affordable. Then, there is the balloon mortgage situation which was probably the single greatest factor that led to the housing crash.

Now some conservatives based on this article and the related ones are falling back to some Keynesian policies. Still, they are vigorously opposing this idea of a liquidity trap. I would say what is happening today is a sort of liquidity trap or at least a similar concept. There's all this "idle money" lying around and it has nowhere productive to go -- so bubbles persist. Some have said that this entire bubble will eventually be cleaned up when it is all absorbed by government debt. That could happen -- and with a very high economic price tag.

Its funny how neither Krugman nor his opponents in this debate want to seriously touch the massive liquid wealth of the richest players. There is the problem.

The greatest wrong was done when the decision by Volker/Greenspan/Paulson was to pump money into the shadow economy/asset bubbles by way of monetary policy instead of pumping money from the wealthy back into the working people's pockets.

But this grand monetary policy experiment did do one thing: It demonstrated that monetary, "supply side"/Trickle-down policy does not work well and that Keynesian "Demand Side" stimulus policy like in the New Deal should be the way forward.

Edit: Yep, we are in a liquidity trap but so is everyone else, even China. Japan was the canary in the coal mine.
